passage: "Ankita, come, sit with your Appachan. You think you're the only one whose eyes blink by themselves? When I was nine, in our village by the backwaters, my eyes blinked and my throat made a little 'hnk' sound. Before each one I felt an itch building, like a sneeze that must come out. In exam week it was worst. My teacher once made me stand at the front and said, 'Thomas, stop this nonsense.' That day I couldn't stop at all. But when I sat mending fishing nets with my father, hours would pass with hardly a blink. My mother never once scolded me for it. She just said, 'It comes and it goes, mone.' And you know, she was right."

qa.q: What was young Thomas doing when his tics nearly disappeared?
qa.a: He was mending fishing nets with his father.

qa.q: How did young Thomas feel when his teacher made him stand at the front?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and tense, and the shame made his tics worse, so he could not stop at all.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped young Thomas more, the teacher's or his mother's?
qa.a: His mother's calm acceptance helped more; she never scolded and said the tics come and go, while the teacher's shaming made them worse.

qa.q: How might Thomas's mother have seen his blinking?
qa.a: She seemed to see it as something that comes and goes, not a fault, and chose to stay calm and accepting.

grounding: An elder recalls childhood tics with urges building before them, worse with stress and shame, easing when absorbed in a task.

passage: The school annual day was running late, the stage lights were blinding, and Hansa, ten, was third in line for the dance. Her nose twitched and she sniffed, once, twice, five times. The urge built in her face like a sneeze that wouldn't come. The girl beside her whispered, "Stop it, it's gross." Hansa's cheeks burned, and the sniffing came faster. Her brother Pankaj, backstage with the props, just handed her the scarf and said, "Your part's great, remember the turn." Then the music started. Hansa spun, stamped, clapped. For four whole minutes, lost in the steps, she didn't sniff once. Afterwards, in the noisy corridor, it started again, but softer.

qa.q: Where was Pankaj during the annual day?
qa.a: He was backstage with the props.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel when the girl beside her said "Stop it"?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed, her cheeks burning, and the sniffing came faster.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do that helped more than commenting on the tic?
qa.a: He ignored the sniffing, handed her the scarf and reminded her about her turn, keeping her focus on the dance.

qa.q: How does Pankaj seem to see his sister's sniffing?
qa.a: He seems to treat it as nothing unusual, keeping his attention on her dance, which suggests quiet acceptance.

grounding: Shows a child's tic building like an urge, rising with excitement and shame, and fading while she is absorbed in dancing.

passage: In their Kolkata flat, Kashish, nine, blinked hard three times and made a small "hm" sound, then did it again. India were two wickets from winning, and the room was shouting. Anjali, his mother, opened her mouth to say "Stop blinking" and closed it; last month she had said it, and he had blinked all evening, near tears. "It's like an itch in my eyes. It has to come out," he had told her. Later that evening he sat at the table drawing his comic about a flying auto-rickshaw. Anjali watched from the kitchen. For forty minutes, absorbed in his pencil, he hardly blinked at all. She made him tea and said nothing about it.

qa.q: What was Kashish's comic about?
qa.a: His comic was about a flying auto-rickshaw.

qa.q: Why did Anjali close her mouth instead of saying "Stop blinking"?
qa.a: She felt worried and remembered that her words last month made him upset and near tears, and made the blinking worse.

qa.q: What did Anjali learn about when Kashish's tics ease?
qa.a: They ease when he is absorbed in something calm like drawing, and rise with excitement and being told to stop.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel when his mother says nothing about the blinking?
qa.a: He may feel relaxed and accepted, able to get on with his comic without shame.

grounding: Shows a child with blinking and sound tics driven by an urge, which rise with excitement and shame and fall when he is absorbed.

passage:
Thursday
Today in maths Manoj copied my head jerk and made the squeaky sound I make. Four boys laughed. I wanted the floor to swallow me. I can't stop it. I told Mumma once, it's like trying not to sneeze.
Then Lata Ma'am put down her chalk. She said, "Rashmi's movements are tics. They are not a choice. Nobody in this class copies them again." That's all she said. Then she went back to fractions. Manoj went red.
At lunch Pooja sat next to me and just talked about her cousin's wedding like nothing happened. She didn't look at my head at all. I ate my whole tiffin.
I still feel sore inside. But less.

qa.q: What did Lata Ma'am say about Rashmi's movements?
qa.a: She said they are tics, not a choice, and nobody in the class copies them again.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when Manoj copied the head jerk?
qa.a: Rashmi felt humiliated and hurt, wishing the floor would swallow her.

qa.q: Why did Lata Ma'am's response work well?
qa.a: It was brief, stated clearly that tics are not a choice, stopped the mocking and then moved on without making a fuss.

qa.q: How does Pooja seem to see Rashmi at lunch?
qa.a: Pooja seems to see Rashmi simply as a friend, not as her tics, chatting about the wedding as if nothing happened.

grounding: Shows a child hurt by a classmate's mimicking of her tics, helped by a teacher's brief explanation and a friend who carries on as normal.

passage: At the bus stop outside the village school near Mandi, two boys jerked their heads sideways every time Charu, eleven, did. They laughed and nudged each other. Charu stared at her shoes, blinking fast, her chest aching. Sharma Sir, walking to his scooter, stopped. "Charu's movements are not something she chooses. Copying her is cruel, and it ends today." The boys shuffled off. Charu's friend Kalyani didn't mention it at all. She just kept telling Charu about the calf born in their cowshed that morning, how it slipped on the straw and stood up again. By the time the bus came, Charu was laughing about the calf, too.

qa.q: What was born in Kalyani's cowshed that morning?
qa.a: A calf was born in the cowshed that morning.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when the boys copied her?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, staring at her shoes with her chest aching.

qa.q: What did Sharma Sir do that helped?
qa.a: He briefly explained that the movements are not a choice, called the copying cruel and stopped it on the spot.

qa.q: How does Kalyani seem to see Charu?
qa.a: Kalyani sees Charu as an ordinary friend to chat with; she never mentions the movements and just talks about the calf.

grounding: Shows a child hurt by mimicking of her tics, helped by a teacher who explains they are not a choice and a friend who simply carries on.

passage: In a Manchester primary school, Bilal, ten, cleared his throat loudly, a tic that came in bursts. During silent reading a girl turned and stared, then another. Someone whispered, "Is he doing it on purpose?" Bilal hunched over his book, face hot. Ms Clarke looked up. "Bilal has tics. His body does them without him choosing, a bit like hiccups. Eyes on your own books, please." The staring stopped. At break Tomas, his friend, handed him the football as usual. "You're in goal first." He didn't mention it at all. Bilal dived for every shot until the bell, and forgot all about the reading room.

qa.q: What did Ms Clarke compare Bilal's tics to?
qa.a: She compared them to hiccups.

qa.q: How did Bilal feel when classmates stared during silent reading?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, hunching over his book with a hot face.

qa.q: Why was Ms Clarke's explanation helpful?
qa.a: It was short and clear, said the tics are not a choice and turned the class's attention back to their own books.

qa.q: How does Tomas treat Bilal at break, and what does it show?
qa.a: Tomas hands him the football and puts him in goal as usual, showing that Bilal is simply his friend.

grounding: Shows a child hurt by stares at his tics, helped by a teacher's brief explanation and a friend who carries on as normal.

passage: "Harish, you think I don't know why you go straight to your room after school? When I was sixteen, I held my tics in all day at school. Shoulder shrugs, a little cough. I'd squeeze my fists under the desk till my nails left marks. Then I'd get home and it would all come out at once, like a pressure cooker, and I'd be so tired I'd fall asleep in my uniform. My father used to shout, 'Tanuja, stop that jerking!' It only got worse. One day my mother said, 'In this house you don't hold anything in.' And she took me to a doctor, who explained what tics are and what options there were. Nobody blamed me after that. So, in this house too, beta, you don't hold anything in."

qa.q: What did Tanuja do under her desk to hold in her tics?
qa.a: She squeezed her fists under the desk till her nails left marks.

qa.q: How did young Tanuja feel after coming home from school?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and self-conscious, releasing all the held-in tics at once and falling asleep in her uniform.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Tanuja cope better?
qa.a: Her mother said she did not have to hold anything in at home and took her to a doctor who explained tics and options, so nobody blamed her.

qa.q: How did Tanuja's mother see her daughter's tics?
qa.a: She saw them as nothing to blame Tanuja for, making home a place where Tanuja did not have to hold anything in, and sought a doctor's explanation.

grounding: An elder recalls suppressing tics at school and releasing them at home, tired and self-conscious, and coping better once not blamed and helped by a doctor's explanation.

passage: The board exam hall was dead silent, and the invigilator kept pacing. Vijay, fifteen, felt the urge to jerk his neck building like a spring. For three hours he pressed his chin down and held it, sweat on his back, one eye on the clock and the other on the long answer he still had to finish. He barely finished. At home he went up to the terrace and let the tics come: neck, shoulder, a sharp sound, over and over. His brother Tarun came up with two glasses of nimbu pani, sat on the parapet and talked about the match. He didn't say "stop." That night their mother said the doctor could see Vijay next week, to explain options since his neck was aching.

qa.q: How long did Vijay hold in his tics in the exam hall?
qa.a: He held them in for three hours.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel during and after the exam?
qa.a: He felt tense and self-conscious during it, and drained afterwards, releasing all the tics on the terrace.

qa.q: What helped Vijay cope after the exam?
qa.a: Tarun kept him company without telling him to stop, and their mother arranged for a doctor to explain options because his neck ached.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun to sit with Vijay on the terrace?
qa.a: Tarun seems relaxed and caring; he chooses to chat about the match so Vijay does not feel watched.

grounding: Shows a teenager suppressing tics in public and releasing them at home, tired and self-conscious, coping better when not blamed, with a doctor to explain options.

passage: At his cousin's wedding in Ahmedabad, Jagdish, fourteen, stood in every family photograph with his hands clasped tight, holding back the shoulder jerk and the throat click. Aunties kept calling, "One more, beta, smile!" By the ninth photo his arms were trembling. In the car home the tics burst out one after another, and he stared out of the window, embarrassed. His older sister Ritu didn't say a word about it. She just passed him a water bottle and put on his favourite song. At home he fell asleep on the sofa. The next day Ritu said, "Your shoulder must hurt. Want to ask the doctor at your check-up about options? No pressure." Jagdish nodded.

qa.q: What did Jagdish hold back during the photographs?
qa.a: He held back the shoulder jerk and the throat click.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel in the car on the way home?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and worn out, staring out of the window as the held-back tics burst out.

qa.q: What did Ritu do right?
qa.a: She did not comment or ask him to stop, gave him water and music, and later gently offered the idea of asking a doctor about options.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel watching Jagdish struggle through the photos?
qa.a: She may feel protective and sympathetic, seeing how hard he worked to hold everything in.

grounding: Shows a teenager suppressing tics in public and releasing them later, tired and embarrassed, and a sibling who does not blame him and mentions a doctor can explain options.

passage:
Monday: On Rehana's first day at the library internship, her head jerked sideways and she made a sharp squeak mid-sentence. A visitor at the counter laughed. Imran, cataloguing beside her, just said, "So the old maps go on shelf C?" and carried on.
Wednesday: At lunch, Rehana's tics came fast, three squeaks in a row. Imran didn't look up from his rice. "Did you finish the map labels? They look great."
Friday: As they locked up, Rehana said, "You've never asked about my tics." Imran shrugged. "Figured you'd tell me if you wanted." She smiled. "I do. They're tics, and they get worse when I'm new somewhere." "Thanks for telling me," he said, and they walked to the bus stop talking about Monday's exhibition.

qa.q: Where do Imran and Rehana work?
qa.a: They work at a library internship.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when she brought up her tics on Friday?
qa.a: She felt accepted and comfortable enough to explain, smiling because Imran had never made an issue of them.

qa.q: Why was Imran's way of responding wise?
qa.a: He never commented, stared or asked her to stop, kept the conversation going and only talked about the tics when she raised them.

qa.q: How does Imran seem to see Rehana's tics?
qa.a: Imran seems to see them as simply part of Rehana, nothing that needs comment, questions or fixing.

grounding: Shows a friend who does not comment, imitate or ask for tics to stop, carries on the conversation and acknowledges them only when the person raises it.

passage: "Chetan, you're nervous about the new intern with tics? Let me tell you what I did wrong at your age. When I was twenty-two, a colleague named Victor used to make a sharp barking sound and twitch his arm. In our first meeting I said, 'Can you please stop that? The client can hear.' He went red and didn't speak for the rest of the day. I felt terrible. After that, I learned: I just carried on talking. I didn't look away, I didn't copy, I didn't ask. Weeks later he said, 'Sarika, thanks for never making it a thing.' Then he told me about it himself, over tea. He became my closest friend in that office. So with your intern: talk about the work. Let them bring it up."

qa.q: What sound did Victor make?
qa.a: He made a sharp barking sound and twitched his arm.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel after asking Victor to stop?
qa.a: She felt terrible and guilty when he went red and stayed silent all day.

qa.q: What choice inside the story built trust between Sarika and Victor?
qa.a: She stopped commenting or asking, carried on normally and let Victor raise his tics when he chose, which later led to friendship.

qa.q: How might Victor have felt when Sarika asked him to stop in front of others?
qa.a: He likely felt humiliated and hurt, which is why he went red and did not speak for the rest of the day.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to respectfully ignore a colleague's tics, carrying on the conversation and acknowledging them only when he raised it.

passage: The café was packed, the project was due at nine the next morning, and Pradeep and Deepika had four slides left. Deepika's vocal tic, a short "hup," came every few seconds, louder when she was stressed. A man at the next table turned and glared. Pradeep didn't look at him or at Deepika's mouth. He kept pointing at the laptop. "This graph needs a title. What about 'Water use by ward'?" Deepika nodded. "Hup. Yes. Good." They finished at eleven. Walking out, she said, "That guy was staring." Pradeep said, "I noticed. Does it bother you when people do that?" "Sometimes. Thanks for just carrying on." "Always," he said.

qa.q: What title did Pradeep suggest for the graph?
qa.a: He suggested 'Water use by ward.'

qa.q: How did Deepika feel about Pradeep carrying on with the work?
qa.a: She felt grateful and accepted, thanking him for just carrying on despite the man's stare.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do that made Deepika feel accepted?
qa.a: He ignored the tic, kept working on the slides and only talked about it when Deepika raised the staring, asking how it felt for her.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when Deepika thanks him?
qa.a: He likely feels glad and a little moved, answering "Always" to show he will keep treating her the same way.

grounding: Shows a friend who does not comment on or stop a person's tics, keeps working with her and acknowledges them only when she raises it, despite a noisy café and a deadline.

subtype: Worry showing as stomach aches and clinging [Actor]
passage: Nursery note, Monday. Mridul, five, said his tummy hurt on arrival, the third Monday running. He clung to his father's leg at the gate and asked, "What if you forget to come? What if the car breaks?" His face was pale, his hands cold. We started a routine: the same goodbye hug, a wave from the window and a picture of his father's car on his cubby. His father will stay five minutes this week, then two next week. By snack time Mridul was eating. Next: share the plan with the family on Friday. — Tenzin

qa.q: What picture did the nursery put on Mridul's cubby?
qa.a: They put a picture of his father's car on his cubby.

qa.q: How was Mridul feeling at the gate, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was frightened and anxious; he said his tummy hurt, clung to his father, asked what-if questions and was pale with cold hands.

qa.q: What steps did Tenzin take to help Mridul?
qa.a: Tenzin set a calm, predictable goodbye routine and a gentle plan where his father stays a shorter time each week.

qa.q: How might Mridul's father feel about the plan?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and reassured that the nursery takes Mridul's fear seriously and has a gentle, clear plan.

grounding: Shows a child whose fear shows as stomach aches, clinging and what-if questions, helped by a calm routine and gentle steps toward separation.

subtype: Worry showing as stomach aches and clinging [Actor]
passage: Every morning before the anganwadi, Abhinav, five, rubbed his tummy and whimpered, "Pet dukh raha hai." His mother, Madhuri, saw his sweaty forehead. "What if the bus doesn't bring me back?" he asked, again and again. She didn't keep him home. She walked him along the canal, singing the same counting song every day. At the gate she gave him her small cloth handkerchief. "Keep it. Give it back at lunch." First he stayed till the story; the next week, until lunch. On Friday he ran out, waving the handkerchief. "Amma, the bus doesn't even come here. You come!"

qa.q: What did Madhuri give Abhinav at the gate?
qa.a: She gave him her small cloth handkerchief.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling before the anganwadi each morning?
qa.a: He was scared and anxious, with a real tummy ache, a sweaty forehead and repeated what-if questions.

qa.q: Why was Madhuri's approach wise?
qa.a: She kept a calm, same routine and used small steps, from story time to lunch, instead of keeping him home.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel when Abhinav runs out waving the handkerchief?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and proud that the gentle steps worked, and amused by his joke about the bus.

grounding: Shows a young child with stomach aches, clinging and what-if questions before school, helped by a calm routine and gentle steps.

subtype: Worry showing as stomach aches and clinging [Actor]
passage: In a Vancouver kindergarten, Aiko, five, cried at the door each morning, holding her grandmother's coat. "What if the fire alarm rings?" The alarm test had terrified her, and now her tummy hurt before class. Her teacher, Ines, spoke calmly. "Your body feels the fear. Shall we look at the alarm together when it's quiet?" On Tuesday they looked at the red bell from the hallway. On Wednesday Aiko touched the wall under it. Each day ended with the same song and hug. By Friday Aiko walked in holding Ines's hand, and her tummy didn't hurt.

qa.q: What did Aiko do on Wednesday?
qa.a: She touched the wall under the alarm bell.

qa.q: Why did Aiko's tummy hurt every morning?
qa.a: She was frightened and worried that the loud fire alarm would ring again, and her body felt the fear.

qa.q: What made Ines's plan work?
qa.a: She used a calm tone, kept a steady routine and took small steps toward the alarm when it was quiet.

qa.q: How might Aiko's grandmother feel on Friday?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and happy to see Aiko walk in holding the teacher's hand without tears.

grounding: Shows a young child whose worry comes out as stomach aches and clinging, helped by a calm routine and gentle steps toward the feared alarm.

passage: In Buenos Aires, Valentina, ten, was invited to her cousin Santiago's birthday sleepover. Her stomach dropped. What if she couldn't sleep? What if she cried in front of everyone? She begged her mother to say she was ill, and when her mother agreed, Valentina felt a huge rush of relief. But the next month she refused a school trip too, and then a friend's afternoon party. Her mother saw the pattern. "Every time we say no, the fear gets bigger. What if you go to Santiago's until nine and I pick you up?" Valentina was scared but agreed. At nine she was laughing so hard over a card game she asked, "Can I stay till ten?"

qa.q: What did Valentina's mother suggest as a first step?
qa.a: She suggested Valentina go to Santiago's until nine and be picked up.

qa.q: How did Valentina feel when she was excused from the sleepover?
qa.a: She felt a huge rush of relief, but that relief made her avoid more things afterwards.

qa.q: Why was the "until nine" plan wiser than staying home?
qa.a: It was a small, supported step toward the fear, so the fear could shrink instead of growing with each avoidance.

qa.q: How might Santiago feel when Valentina asks to stay till ten?
qa.a: He may feel happy that his cousin is enjoying his party and wants to stay longer.

grounding: Shows a child who avoids a sleepover and feels relief when excused, the avoidance growing, and a supportive small step that helps.

passage: On the morning of the maths test, Mahima, eleven, was in the school sick room again, clutching her stomach. Gopika, the school nurse, checked her gently; she had been there on the last three test days. Every time she was sent home, Mahima's shoulders dropped with relief. Gopika sat beside her. "When you miss tests, does the fear get smaller or bigger next time?" Mahima whispered, "Bigger." Gopika phoned her parents and spoke to her class teacher that same morning. The plan: Mahima would sit the first half of today's test in the quiet room next to the office, with a glass of water, and then decide. She finished the whole paper. "It was hard," she said, "but I did it."

qa.q: Where did Mahima sit the test?
qa.a: She sat it in the quiet room next to the office.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel whenever she was sent home on test days?
qa.a: She felt relief, her shoulders dropping, but the fear grew bigger each time.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that was wise?
qa.a: She gently helped Mahima notice the avoidance pattern, involved her parents and teacher, and set up a small, supported step to face the test.

qa.q: How might Mahima's class teacher see her after she finished the paper?
qa.a: The teacher may see her as braver and more capable than her sick-room visits suggested.

grounding: Shows a child avoiding exam days and relieved when excused, with the relief feeding avoidance, and a nurse arranging a supported small step instead.

passage:
Saturday: Dilnaz, nine, refused to go to Usha Aunty's daughter's birthday party. "Too many people. What if I get lost?" Ammi let her stay home, and Dilnaz felt light with relief. But on Monday she refused the school picnic too.
Wednesday: Ammi called Usha Aunty. "She gets scared in crowds. Could she come early to help set up, before everyone arrives, for the next party?" Usha laughed kindly. "Rimi's other birthday party is at her grandmother's on Sunday. Come at four."
Sunday: Dilnaz arrived at four, blew up twelve balloons and hung streamers with Rimi. When the guests came, she already knew every corner of the room. She stayed until the cake, and then until the games.

qa.q: How many balloons did Dilnaz blow up?
qa.a: She blew up twelve balloons.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when Ammi let her skip the first party?
qa.a: She felt light with relief, but then she refused the school picnic too, so the fear was spreading.

qa.q: What small step helped Dilnaz go to the party?
qa.a: Arriving early to help set up before guests came, so the room felt familiar and safe.

qa.q: How might Usha Aunty feel seeing Dilnaz stay until the games?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and warm that her small help made the party possible for Dilnaz.

grounding: Shows a child whose avoidance of parties brings relief and spreads, and how a supportive small step helps her take part.

passage: In a Prague primary school, Jana noticed that Ada, eight, asked "Is this right?" after every single sum, sometimes six times a lesson. Twice this week her eyes had filled with tears over a small mistake. At break Jana sat beside her. "You seem worried a lot lately. What's it like?" Ada whispered, "What if I get everything wrong and Mama is sad?" Jana kept her voice soft. "That sounds heavy. Thank you for telling me." That afternoon she phoned Ada's parents. They agreed together: Ada would get a star card to check her work herself, Jana would check in once each lesson, not every sum, and her parents would ask about her day, not her marks.

qa.q: How many times a lesson did Ada sometimes ask "Is this right?"
qa.a: She sometimes asked it six times a lesson.

qa.q: How did Jana feel about the pattern she noticed in Ada?
qa.a: Jana felt concerned and caring, noticing the constant questions and tears and choosing to gently ask about them.

qa.q: Why was the plan with Ada's parents a wise approach?
qa.a: It took the worry seriously without dismissing it, and reduced constant reassurance so it would not feed the worry.

qa.q: How might Ada feel about the star card plan?
qa.a: Ada may feel calmer and more capable, checking her own work and trusting a warm check-in instead of constant reassurance.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a child who is tearful and constantly seeking reassurance, using gentle questions, a calm tone and a plan with the family.

passage: At the swimming club, coach Vaibhav noticed Hafsa, ten, sitting silent on the bench while the others splashed. Before every session she asked, "Will I drown? Are you sure? Are you sure?" Last week she had cried in the changing room. He didn't say "Don't be silly," and he didn't let her skip forever. He crouched beside her. "You look worried. What's the scariest part?" "The deep end," she said. He nodded slowly. "That's a real feeling. Thanks for telling me." At pickup he spoke with her mother. They agreed: shallow end only for two weeks, the same warm-up every time, and Hafsa could hold the rail whenever she liked. Next session she slid in first.

qa.q: What did Hafsa say was the scariest part?
qa.a: She said the deep end was the scariest part.

qa.q: How did coach Vaibhav feel seeing Hafsa silent on the bench?
qa.a: He seemed concerned and gentle, noticing her worry and crouching down to ask about it calmly.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav avoid both dismissing and feeding Hafsa's worry?
qa.a: He did not call her silly or let her skip forever; he listened, then made a small, steady plan with her mother.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel about starting in the shallow end?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel safer and braver, which shows when she slides in first at the next session.

grounding: Shows an adult noticing a quiet, tearful child who keeps seeking reassurance, responding with gentle questions, a calm tone and a plan with the family.

passage: I'm Kishore, Tejas's Mama; I've lived with my sister's family since spring. For the last few weeks Tejas, nine, has been very quiet at dinner. He asks, "Mummy is definitely coming home at seven? Definitely?" three or four times a night. On Sunday I found him crying on the stairs, but he said nothing was wrong. I can't know what he's thinking. I didn't say "Stop worrying," and I didn't keep promising either. I sat down and said, "Something seems to be bothering you. I'm here." He leaned on my arm. That night I told my sister what I'd seen, and we arranged to meet his class teacher together on Tuesday to make a plan.

qa.q: What time does Tejas keep asking about?
qa.a: He keeps asking whether Mummy is definitely coming home at seven.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel finding Tejas crying on the stairs?
qa.a: Kishore felt concerned and tender, choosing to sit quietly with him rather than dismiss or feed the worry.

qa.q: What steps did Kishore take that were wise?
qa.a: He spoke calmly and gently, stayed with Tejas, told his sister that night and planned a meeting with the class teacher.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when he leaned on Kishore's arm?
qa.a: He may have felt comforted and safe, even if he couldn't yet say what was wrong.

grounding: Shows an adult relative noticing a quiet, tearful child seeking reassurance, responding gently and making a plan with the family and school.

passage: At the boarding school, Ishita, fifteen, had not slept properly in five weeks. At lights-out her mind raced: What if I fail chemistry? What if this headache is something serious? What if Riya is angry with me? She checked her marks portal four times a night. In the day she snapped at her roommate for humming and cried in the washroom after a class test. The house mother noticed her dark eyes and walked her to the counsellor, Kamal Sir, that afternoon. Ishita said, "I'm just stressed, like everyone." Kamal Sir listened, then said gently, "Five weeks without sleep and crying every day is bigger than normal exam stress. Let's work on this together." They set a time for the next day, and he called her parents with her.

qa.q: How long had Ishita been sleeping badly?
qa.a: She had not slept properly in five weeks.

qa.q: How was Ishita feeling in the weeks before seeing the counsellor?
qa.a: She felt tense and constantly worried, with racing what-if thoughts, and it showed as irritability and crying.

qa.q: Why was seeing Kamal Sir the right step?
qa.a: The worry had lasted weeks and was limiting her sleep and life, so a counsellor could help, and he involved her parents with her.

qa.q: How might Ishita's roommate have seen her snapping about the humming?
qa.a: The roommate might have felt hurt or confused, not knowing the irritability came from weeks of worry and no sleep.

grounding: Shows a teenager who cannot sleep and spirals over grades, health and friends, seeming irritable, and how lasting worry calls for a counsellor.

passage:
Dear Noor,
I'm sorry I snapped at you on Friday. You didn't deserve it. I want to explain.
For about three months my head hasn't been quiet. At night it runs through lists: what if I fail the unit test, what if my heart is beating weird, what if you and the others are only pretending to like me. I lie awake till two. I check my pulse. Then I'm grumpy all day, and I skip football because I'm too tired.
I thought it was normal nerves. But it's been too long and it's stopping me doing things. So on Monday I went to the school counsellor. It was awkward, but I'm going again Thursday.
I just wanted you to know it wasn't you.
Joseph

qa.q: How long has Joseph's head not been quiet?
qa.a: For about three months.

qa.q: How has Joseph been feeling at night?
qa.a: Joseph has been anxious and tense, lying awake till two with racing what-if thoughts about tests, health and friends.

qa.q: Why did Joseph decide to see the counsellor?
qa.a: Joseph realised it was more than ordinary nerves because it had lasted months and was stopping everyday things like football.

qa.q: How might Noor feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Noor may feel relieved that the snapping wasn't personal, and caring toward Joseph for sharing something hard.

grounding: Shows a teenager tense, sleepless and spiralling about grades, health and friends, seeming irritable, and seeing a counsellor when it lasts and limits life.

passage: Rajni, you asked why I disappeared from the dance group last term. Okay. I'm Deepika, I was fifteen, and I couldn't switch my brain off. Every night: what if I fail maths, what if this cough is serious, what if everyone's talking about me in the group chat? I'd lie there till three, heart thumping. In the mornings I snapped at Mummy over nothing. I stopped going to dance because I was so tired and so sure I'd mess up. I kept telling myself it was just exam stress. But it went on for months. Finally my class teacher noticed and walked me to the school counsellor. Talking to her every week helped me see the loops. I'm back at dance now. That's why.

qa.q: What time would Deepika lie awake until?
qa.a: Deepika would lie awake till three.

qa.q: How was Deepika feeling during those months?
qa.a: She felt tense and anxious, with racing what-ifs, and was irritable and exhausted.

qa.q: What made this more than exam stress, and what helped?
qa.a: It lasted months and stopped her dancing; her class teacher took her to the school counsellor, and weekly talks helped.

qa.q: How might Rajni have seen Deepika's disappearance from dance?
qa.a: Rajni may have felt confused or hurt, not knowing Deepika was struggling with constant worry.

grounding: Shows a teenager tense, sleepless and spiralling about grades, health and friends, whose lasting worry leads to talking with a counsellor.

passage: In Accra, the night before the swim trials, Esther, sixteen, sat on the steps outside her building, breathing fast. "My hands won't stop shaking. What if I freeze on the block?" Her friend Gabriel sat beside her. He didn't say "just relax." He said, "That sounds awful. Tell me what's happening." He listened for a long time. Then: "One small thing. Tomorrow, just walk to the block. Only that." She did, and she swam. Over the next weeks he walked with her every evening and nagged her about sleeping by ten. When her panic kept coming back before every race, he said, "I think this needs more than me," and went with her to book an appointment with the school counsellor.

qa.q: What did Gabriel suggest as one small step?
qa.a: He suggested she just walk to the block tomorrow, only that.

qa.q: How did Gabriel seem to feel when he said "I think this needs more than me"?
qa.a: He seemed concerned and caring, honest enough to see that Esther's lasting panic needed a professional, not only a friend.

qa.q: What did Gabriel do that shows steady support?
qa.a: He listened without saying relax, helped her take one small step, encouraged walks and sleep, and helped her book the counsellor when the anxiety lasted.

qa.q: How might Esther see Gabriel after the trials?
qa.a: She may see him as a trusted friend who took her fear seriously and stayed with her.

grounding: Shows a supportive friend who listens without saying just relax, helps with one small step, encourages sleep and movement, and helps find a professional when anxiety lasts.

passage: After three weeks off sick, Kamal, fifteen, stood frozen at the school gate. "Everyone will stare. What if I've missed too much?" Bhavna, from his class, had come to meet him there. She didn't say "It's nothing, just come in." She said, "That's a lot to walk into. What would make it smaller?" They agreed on one thing: the side gate, straight to the library for first period only. They sat there together while she caught him up on history. Each evening that week she texted, "Walk done?" because he'd said walks helped him sleep. When he was still dreading every morning a fortnight later, she asked, "Can I come with you to the counsellor?" He nodded.

qa.q: Which period did Kamal first go to the library for?
qa.a: He went to the library for first period only.

qa.q: How did Bhavna seem to feel waiting at the gate with Kamal?
qa.a: She seemed calm and caring, patient enough to ask what would make it smaller instead of hurrying him.

qa.q: How did Bhavna support Kamal in a steady way?
qa.a: She listened without brushing it off, helped him take one small step, encouraged his evening walks and offered to go with him to the counsellor when the dread lasted.

qa.q: What would change if Bhavna had said "It's nothing, just come in"?
qa.a: Kamal would probably feel dismissed and more anxious, and might have turned back from the gate instead of taking a small step.

grounding: Shows a steady friend who listens without dismissing, helps one small step, encourages movement and sleep, and helps involve a counsellor when anxiety lasts.

passage:
Dear Tanvir,
Masi told me you've been lying awake worrying about the new school in Pune. I'm not going to tell you to relax. When I moved in Class 9, people kept saying that, and it only made me feel worse.
So here's one small step: next week, go and just walk around the new school gate with Masi. That's all. Look at it. Find the canteen.
Also, sleep. I know. But put the phone away by ten, and keep playing cricket in the evenings. It really helps the churning stomach.
If the worry doesn't shrink after a few weeks, tell Masi, and we'll help you find a counsellor. That's not a big scary thing. I saw one, too.
Call me anytime.
Mridul

qa.q: What small step does Mridul suggest for next week?
qa.a: To walk around the new school gate with Masi, look at it and find the canteen.

qa.q: How does Mridul feel about being told to relax?
qa.a: Mridul felt misunderstood and worse when people said it during a school move, so Mridul chooses not to say it to Tanvir.

qa.q: What makes Mridul's letter steady support?
qa.a: It avoids saying relax, suggests one small step, encourages sleep and cricket, and points to a counsellor if the worry lasts.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel reading that Mridul also saw a counsellor?
qa.a: Tanvir may feel less alone and less ashamed, seeing that getting help is normal.

grounding: Shows a supportive cousin who avoids saying just relax, suggests one small step, encourages sleep and movement, and offers help finding a counsellor if anxiety lasts.

passage:
Dear Sonali,
I've been in Bengaluru for five weeks now, and I keep telling everyone the new job is "great." It isn't great. Not the job, the job is fine. It's me.
Every morning in the metro my thoughts race: What if I mess up the client call? What if they realise they hired the wrong person? My chest goes tight. At lunch I smile and nod and then cry in the washroom.
I haven't told anyone at work. I've barely told Mum.
But you always said telling someone is half the battle. So I'm telling you. And tomorrow I have an appointment with a counsellor through the office helpline. I booked it last night before I could chicken out.
Wish me luck?
Elizabeth

qa.q: How long has Elizabeth been in Bengaluru?
qa.a: Elizabeth has been in Bengaluru for five weeks.

qa.q: How has Elizabeth been feeling in the new job?
qa.a: Elizabeth has felt anxious and overwhelmed, with racing thoughts and a tight chest, while hiding it behind smiles.

qa.q: What steps is Elizabeth taking that show strength?
qa.a: Sharing it honestly with Sonali and booking a counsellor through the office helpline early, before it grows.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sonali may feel worried but also touched and proud that Elizabeth trusted Sonali with this and took a step to get help.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new city and job with racing thoughts, a tight chest and fear of not coping, who shares it and seeks professional help early.

passage: Alka didi, you asked why I called you at midnight in my first month. So, I'm Divyansh, your kid brother, and I'd just moved to Pune for college, and I was sure I was going to fail. My thoughts raced all night: what if I can't keep up, what if I run out of money for the mess, what if everyone finds out I'm not as smart as they think? My chest felt tight, like a belt was pulled round it. In class I laughed and acted fine. I didn't want to be the weak one. Then that night I called you, and you just listened. The next day I went to the college counselling centre. It wasn't weak. Honestly, it was the bravest thing I did that year.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh move for college?
qa.a: Divyansh moved to Pune for college.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel in his first month at college?
qa.a: Divyansh felt panicky and afraid of not coping, with racing thoughts and a tight chest, while hiding it.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that helped, and why was it a strength?
qa.a: Divyansh called his sister and then went to the college counselling centre early, which took courage rather than weakness.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt getting the midnight call?
qa.a: Alka may have been worried but glad her brother reached out, and she chose to listen.

grounding: Shows a young adult new to a city with racing thoughts, a tight chest and fear of not coping, who shares it and seeks professional help early as a strength.

passage:
Week one: Imran, twenty-one, started his first job in Chennai. He didn't know the language well, the office was huge, and every night his thoughts raced. What if I can't do this? What if I have to go home? At work he smiled and said, "All good."
Week two: On the crowded train one morning his chest went tight and he got off two stops early, shaking. At lunch his colleague Keerthana asked, "You okay? You look pale." For once he didn't say fine. "Not really." She listened, then showed him the company's free counselling line.
Week four: Imran has had two sessions. He still worries, but he knows what's happening in his body. He told Keerthana, "Asking was the strongest thing I've done here."

qa.q: Where did Imran start his first job?
qa.a: He started his first job in Chennai.

qa.q: How did Imran feel on the crowded train in week two?
qa.a: He felt panicky and frightened, his chest tight, so he got off two stops early, shaking.

qa.q: What did Imran do that helped him cope?
qa.a: He told Keerthana honestly that he was not okay and then used the counselling line early, attending sessions.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Imran says asking was the strongest thing he's done?
qa.a: She may feel glad and touched that her question and the counselling line made a difference.

grounding: Shows a young adult new to a city and job with racing thoughts and a tight chest, hiding it, then sharing and seeking professional help early.
